name: Rylands Papyrus 457

date.label: 2nd century
date.summary: Roberts (1935): first half of the 2nd century. Orsini & Clarysse (2012): 125–175. Nongbri (2005): comparable hands run into the late 2nd and early 3rd centuries, so a later date cannot be ruled out.

holding.library: John Rylands Research Institute and Library, University of Manchester

contents_summary: John 18:31–33 (front) and 18:37–38 (back). A scrap about the size of a credit card (8.9 × 6.4 cm) from a codex, not a scroll.
dating_evidence: Only about a hundred letters survive. The hand is a fairly careful, rounded book script with some decorative hooks, written by someone used to copying literary texts. Every proposed date comes from comparing these letters with dated documents; there is no archaeological context, because the fragment was bought from a dealer. That it comes from a codex, not a roll, fits a Christian book but does not narrow the date.

scholarly_positions.claim: First half of the 2nd century, from comparison with documentary papyri of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries. Roberts reported that Kenyon, Schubart and Bell agreed.
About 170, give or take 25 years.
Comparable hands appear in documents dated to the later 2nd and early 3rd centuries, so no honest range can stop at 150. The 2020 article also publishes new details on how the fragment was acquired.
Places 𝔓52 in its ‘graphic stream’ and concludes that a range across the 2nd century and possibly into the 3rd is defensible.
Mid-2nd century; argues the similar P.Egerton 2 should be dated early too, and that later datings over-correct.
A related question: whether the scribe abbreviated Jesus’ name as a ‘sacred name’ (nomen sacrum). Tuckett doubts it can be shown; Hurtado argues it is probable from line lengths and scribal practice.

provenance: Bought in Egypt in 1920 by Bernard Grenfell for the Rylands Library; identified and published by Colin H. Roberts in 1935. Exact find-spot unknown.
summary: Often called the earliest surviving piece of the New Testament. It is also the best-known example of how hard it is to date handwriting: the famous early date is one proposal among several.

name: Papyrus Bodmer II

date.label: c. 200
date.summary: Martin (editor, 1956): c. 200. Hunger (1960): first half of the 2nd century. Nongbri (2014): 4th century is equally possible. INTF: c. 200.

holding.shelfmark: P. Bodmer II (+ one leaf at the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin)

contents_summary: A nearly complete codex of John 1–14; chapters 15–21 survive only as damaged fragments. John 18:31 lies inside the surviving range, but which letters of it are legible should be checked against the facsimile.
dating_evidence: A large, rounded, carefully spaced hand, much more text than 𝔓52 and so more letters to compare. The codex is thought to belong to the ‘Bodmer papyri’, a group of books apparently found together near Dishna in Upper Egypt. Many of the other books in that group are 4th century or later, which matters if they were buried together.

scholarly_positions.claim: First editor: about 200.
First half of the 2nd century, from comparison with early documentary hands.
Among the scholars arguing for a 2nd-century date.
Comparable hands continue into the 4th century, and the book’s likely find context points the same way; a 4th-century date is at least as plausible.
Revised to the late 3rd or early 4th century.

provenance: Acquired by the collector Martin Bodmer in the 1950s, likely part of the ‘Bodmer papyri’ find associated with the region of Dishna, Upper Egypt.
summary: The most complete early copy of John. The scribe made many corrections, which lets scholars watch a copyist at work.

to_check: Direct Vatican viewer URL (colour images are online at DigiVatLib; CSNTM also has facsimile images)

scholarly_positions.claim: First editors: 175–225.
Late 3rd or early 4th century (about 250–325).
Palaeography and codicology fit the 4th century at least as well; a 4th-century date is equally likely, if not more likely.
Studies the scribe’s habits and identifies later corrections and marginal notes in 4th- or 5th-century hands.

name: Papyrus Bodmer XIV–XV (Hanna Papyrus 1, Mater Verbi)

date.label: c. 200–225 (INTF)
date.summary: Editors: 175–225. Turner: c. 225–275. Orsini & Clarysse: 200–250. Orsini (2015): 3rd/4th c. Nongbri (2016): 4th c. equally or more likely. Leuven Database: 275–325.

contents_summary: Luke 3:18–24:53 and John 1:1–15:10, with gaps; John 1:1–18 complete.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script, an upright, elegant, carefully spaced majuscule. The first editors compared it with Oxyrhynchus papyri that were themselves dated only by palaeography, so the chain never reaches a securely dated document (Nongbri 2016). The closest securely dated match proposed so far is P.Herm. 4 and 5 from the 320s. Its tall, narrow format (about 26 × 13 cm, Turner’s Group 8) matches codices of the 4th century such as some Nag Hammadi books, and it belongs to the Bodmer find, most of whose books are 4th–5th century. Its text is extremely close to Codex Vaticanus, which some read as evidence for an early form of that text and Nongbri reads as consistent with a 4th-century date. Later corrections and notes in 4th- or 5th-century hands show it was still in use then (Royse 2008).
provenance: Part of the Bodmer papyri acquired by Martin Bodmer in the 1950s, probably from the Dishna region of Upper Egypt. Sold in 2006 and donated to the Vatican Library; renamed Hanna Papyrus 1 (Mater Verbi).
summary: The earliest near-complete copy of Luke and one of the two great early papyri of John. Its text is almost identical to Codex Vaticanus.

name: Codex Vaticanus

date.label: 4th century
date.summary: 4th century, usually placed in its first half.

contents_summary: Gospels, Acts, Catholic Epistles and Paul (to Hebrews 9:14). John is complete.
dating_evidence: Early Biblical majuscule with almost no ornament, three columns per page, and no Eusebian section numbers (it uses an older system of chapter divisions). These features are the main reasons it is usually placed at or before the middle of the 4th century.

scholarly_positions.claim: Made alongside Sinaiticus, probably at Caesarea, around the 330s.
A key example of Biblical majuscule in its mature form.

provenance: Recorded in the Vatican Library’s catalogue since the 15th century; how it arrived is not known.
summary: Probably the oldest nearly complete Greek Bible. Its text of John is very close to the early papyri, especially 𝔓75.

name: Codex Sinaiticus

date.label: 4th century
date.summary: Mid-4th century; a date in the 330s–360s is widely accepted.

contents_summary: Complete New Testament, plus much of the Greek Old Testament. John 18:31 is on a fully preserved page.
dating_evidence: Biblical majuscule in its ‘canonical’ form: letters fill a square frame, round letters are circles, strokes are nearly even in thickness and there is little ornament. The Eusebian section numbers in the Gospels give a ‘not before’ date in the early 4th century. Milne and Skeat identified the scribes and used features of their work to argue for the mid-4th century.

scholarly_positions.claim: Mid-4th century, based on the scribes, their corrections and the apparatus.
Suggests Sinaiticus and Vaticanus were made at Caesarea around the time Constantine ordered fifty Bibles from Eusebius (c. 330s).
Mid-4th century.

The secure evidence allows anywhere from about 300 to about 425: the Eusebian apparatus sets the lower limit, and cursive marginal notes resemble documents into the early 5th century. Calls for radiocarbon testing.

provenance: Removed from St Catherine’s Monastery, Sinai, by Constantin von Tischendorf in 1844 and 1859; the circumstances of the 1859 removal remain disputed. Sold by the Soviet government to the British Museum in 1933.
summary: One of the two oldest nearly complete Bibles. Its leaves are split between London, Leipzig, St Catherine’s Monastery and St Petersburg, and the whole book has been reunited online.

scholarly_positions.claim: About 400; argues for Berytus (Beirut), a centre of Latin legal study in the Greek East, as a possible place of origin. Others have proposed Gaul, southern Italy, Egypt or Palestine.

name: Codex Bezae Cantabrigiensis

date.label: c. 400 (Parker); 5th c. (INTF)
date.summary: Parker (1992): about 400. INTF: 5th century. Place of origin is more debated than the date.

contents_summary: Greek–Latin Gospels and Acts on facing pages, with gaps. Greek John lacks 1:16–3:26; 18:14–20:13 is a later supplement.
dating_evidence: Dated from its two scripts: Greek on the left page and Latin on the right, both written by one scribe whose letterforms mix Greek and Latin habits. The text is laid out in sense-lines. Parker’s full study of the scribe, the layout and the later correctors puts it around 400. Eleven successive correctors, working from about the 6th to the 12th century, show its long use.
provenance: At the monastery of St Irenaeus in Lyon in the 16th century; taken by Theodore Beza after the Huguenot sack of Lyon in 1562 and given by him to Cambridge University in 1581.
summary: The chief Greek witness to the ‘Western’ text, famous for its many additions and differences, especially in Acts.

name: Codex Washingtonianus (Freer Gospels)

holding.library: National Museum of Asian Art (Freer Gallery), Smithsonian

contents_summary: The four Gospels in the ‘Western’ order Matthew, John, Luke, Mark. John 14:26–16:7 is missing; John 18 survives. John 1:1–5:11 is on a replacement quire, usually dated to the 7th century.
dating_evidence: Its script is not the Biblical majuscule of the great codices, so the usual comparisons work less well. Its unusual script and the likelihood that it was copied from several exemplars make it hard to pin down more tightly than the late 4th or 5th century.

scholarly_positions.claim: First editor; late 4th to 5th century.
A collection of new studies of the Freer manuscripts, including their palaeography and codicology.

provenance: Bought by Charles Lang Freer from a dealer in Egypt in December 1906.
summary: Famous for an extra saying of Jesus after Mark 16:14 (the ‘Freer Logion’). Its text changes character from book to book, suggesting it was copied from several different exemplars.
to_check: Date of the replacement quire containing John 1:1–5:11 (usually given as 7th century)

name: Codex Alexandrinus
contents_summary: Greek Old and New Testament, with gaps. In John only 6:50–8:52 is missing.
dating_evidence: A later phase of Biblical majuscule: more contrast between thick and thin strokes, some ornament, and enlarged initials standing out in the margin. It contains Athanasius’s Letter to Marcellinus and has the Eusebian apparatus, both pointing after the mid-4th century.

scholarly_positions.claim: The fullest study of its codicology, scribes and palaeography in the Gospels.

provenance: Given by Cyril Lucaris, Patriarch of Constantinople, to King Charles I of England; arrived in 1627.
summary: The third of the great early Bibles. In the Gospels it is an early witness to the form of text that later became standard in Byzantine manuscripts.

name: Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus
contents_summary: Parts of every New Testament book. In John, 18:36–20:25 is lost, but 18:31 survives just before the gap.
dating_evidence: A palimpsest, so the Bible text must be read beneath the later writing. Its single-column Biblical majuscule is usually compared with Codex Alexandrinus, hence a 5th-century date.

scholarly_positions.claim: First deciphered and published the underlying New Testament text.
Re-examined the manuscript and Tischendorf’s readings.

provenance: Brought to Italy in the 16th century and then to France with Catherine de’ Medici’s library.
summary: A palimpsest: in the 12th century the Bible text was scraped off and the parchment reused for sermons of Ephrem the Syrian. The faint lower Bible text was deciphered by Tischendorf in the 1840s.

name: Uncial 087

holding.library: National Library of Russia and St Catherine’s Monastery
holding.city: St Petersburg, Russia and Sinai, Egypt

contents_summary: Three leaves: Matthew 1:23–2:2, 19:3–8, 21:19–24 and John 18:29–35.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script alone; there is no colophon or find context. No dedicated dating study was found, so the date is the INTF catalogue’s and should be treated as a century-wide estimate.
provenance: Part of the codex was taken from Sinai to Russia by Porfiry Uspensky in the 1850s; the rest remains at St Catherine’s.
summary: A few leaves of a large, handsome 6th-century Gospel book whose pages are now split between Sinai and St Petersburg.

scholarly_positions.claim: Treats the purple codices as late examples of Biblical majuscule.

name: Codex Petropolitanus Purpureus

holding.library: National Library of Russia (most leaves); others in Patmos, the Vatican, London, Vienna and elsewhere

dating_evidence: A luxury book on purple-dyed parchment, written in silver ink with the sacred names in gold. It is dated with the other purple Gospel codices (023 O, 042 Σ, 043 Φ) to the 6th century, from their late form of Biblical majuscule and their deluxe production.
provenance: Dispersed across several libraries; acquisition history to be documented.
summary: One of the imperial-style purple Gospel books of the 6th century, now split across several countries.

name: P. Colt 4

date.label: 7th century
date.summary: Palaeographic dates range from the 6th to around 700. INTF: 7th century.

contents_summary: Fragments of John 16:29–19:26. Fragments 11–15 preserve John 18:23–27, 31, 34–35 and 37.
dating_evidence: Unusually for a papyrus, it has an archaeological context. It was excavated at Nessana in the Negev together with documents that carry dates in the 6th and 7th centuries, which supports the palaeographic date.

scholarly_positions.claim: Editors of the Nessana literary papyri.
7th century.

provenance: Excavated in the 1930s at Nessana (Auja el-Hafir) in the Negev by the Colt Archaeological Expedition.
summary: A late papyrus codex, from a time when most Gospel books were on parchment. Evidence that papyrus kept being used for Christian books well after late antiquity.

name: Uncial 0109
contents_summary: Two leaves: John 16:30–17:9 and 18:31–40. Our verse is the first line of the second leaf.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script alone; there is no colophon or find context. No dedicated dating study was found, so the date is the INTF catalogue’s and should be treated as a century-wide estimate.
provenance: Part of the Berlin papyrus collection; its find-spot is not recorded here and needs checking.
summary: Two leaves from a Gospel of John, now in Berlin’s papyrus collection. A small but real witness to how John was being copied in the 7th century.

name: Codex Climaci Rescriptus (Greek Gospels)

date.label: 8th century
date.summary: Palaeographically 7th or 8th century; INTF dates it to the 8th.

holding.library: Museum of the Bible (Green Collection); further leaves at St Catherine’s Monastery

contents_summary: Scattered parts of all four Gospels. For John 18 the surviving text includes 18:1–9, 11–13, 18–24, 28–29, 31 and 36 onward.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script alone; there is no colophon or find context. No dedicated dating study was found, so the date is the INTF catalogue’s and should be treated as a century-wide estimate.
provenance: In the Green Collection since around 2010; eight more leaves were among the 1975 ‘New Finds’ at Sinai.
summary: Another palimpsest: the Greek Gospel text lies underneath a Syriac copy of John Climacus’s ‘Ladder of Divine Ascent’, which gave the codex its name.

name: Codex Basilensis
contents_summary: The four Gospels with a few gaps in Luke. John is complete.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s.
provenance: Given to the Dominicans of Basel by Cardinal John of Ragusa around the time of the Council of Basel (1430s).
summary: One of the oldest near-complete examples of the Byzantine text of the Gospels, the form that dominates later manuscripts.

name: Codex Regius

date.label: 8th century
date.summary: INTF: 8th century. Some scholars prefer the 9th.

contents_summary: The four Gospels with some gaps. In John only 21:15–25 is missing.
dating_evidence: A late, somewhat irregular majuscule. The INTF places it in the 8th century; some specialists prefer the 9th, which is why its timeline bar is long.

scholarly_positions.claim: 8th century.

provenance: In the French royal library since at least the 17th century.
summary: A carelessly written but textually important manuscript: its text often agrees with Codex Vaticanus, and it gives two alternative endings of Mark.

name: Uncial 0234

holding.library: owner not recorded in the sources checked

contents_summary: Published lists give Matthew 28:11–15 and John 1:4–8, 20–24; one apparatus summary also cites it at John 1:18.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script alone; there is no colophon or find context. No dedicated dating study was found, so the date is the INTF catalogue’s and should be treated as a century-wide estimate.
provenance: To be established.
summary: A small 8th-century fragment.

name: Uncial 047
contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps. John breaks off at 18:34, so 18:31 is among the last surviving verses.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s.
provenance: Part of the Robert Garrett collection given to Princeton.
summary: Written in a cross shape on some pages. The text is Byzantine.

name: Uncial 054
contents_summary: Six leaves with John 16:3–19:41 (published lists vary on the exact starting verse), accompanied by a commentary.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s.
provenance: Came to the Vatican Library with the Barberini family’s manuscripts in 1902.
summary: A short run of John with commentary, bound into a later volume in the Barberini collection.

name: Uncial 0211

date.label: 9th century
date.summary: Earlier palaeographic assessments placed it in the 7th century; INTF now dates it to the 9th.

holding.library: Korneli Kekelidze Georgian National Centre of Manuscripts

contents_summary: A complete text of the four Gospels.
dating_evidence: Palaeographers once placed it in the 7th century; the INTF now dates it to the 9th. Without a colophon, the gap reflects how differently late majuscule hands can be read.

scholarly_positions.claim: 9th century (earlier assessments: 7th).

provenance: Held in Georgia’s national manuscript collection alongside Codex Koridethi.
summary: A complete Gospel book written in majuscule, with a Byzantine text.

name: Codex Seidelianus I

holding.library: British Library (main part); Trinity College, Cambridge (one leaf)

contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps. In John, 18:5–19 and 19:4–27 are missing; 18:31 survives between the two gaps.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s.
provenance: Brought from the East by Andreas Erasmus Seidel; later owned by Johann Christoph Wolf, and eventually acquired for the Harley collection in London.
summary: A Byzantine Gospel book brought to the West in the early 18th century.

name: Codex Seidelianus II
contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps. In John, 9:30–10:25, 18:2–18 and 20:12–25 are missing; 18:31 survives.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. provenance: Brought west by Seidel, later owned by Johann Christoph Wolf, and now in Hamburg.
summary: The companion of 011, also brought west by Seidel. A Byzantine text.

name: Codex Cyprius
contents_summary: The four Gospels, complete.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). name: Codex Campianus
contents_summary: The four Gospels, complete.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). name: Codex Nanianus
contents_summary: The four Gospels, complete.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. name: Codex Macedoniensis
contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps. In John only 20:27–21:17 is missing.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. name: Codex Koridethi

holding.library: Korneli Kekelidze Georgian National Centre of Manuscripts

contents_summary: The four Gospels; the gaps are all in Matthew.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s.
provenance: Named for Koridethi, near the Black Sea, where it was kept in the Middle Ages. Found in 1853 in a village in the Caucasus.

name: Codex Petropolitanus
contents_summary: The four Gospels with small gaps. In John, 6:15–35, 8:6–39 and 9:21–10:3 are missing, and 21:22–25 was added later; 18:31 is original.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. name: Codex Athous Dionysiou
contents_summary: The four Gospels, complete.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). name: Codex Sangallensis 48

date.label: 9th century
date.summary: 9th century; the library dates it to around 850.

contents_summary: The four Gospels in Greek with a Latin translation written word-for-word above the lines. In John, 19:17–35 is missing; 18:31 survives.

name: Codex Mosquensis II
contents_summary: The four Gospels. The majuscule hand stops at John 8:39; the rest is a 13th-century minuscule supplement.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s.
provenance: In Moscow since at least the 18th century.
summary: A 9th-century Gospel book completed centuries later in minuscule.

name: Uncial 050 (John with commentary)

holding.library: National Library of Greece; Dionysiou Monastery; State Historical Museum; Christ Church

dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s. Its layout, short passages of Gospel text each followed by commentary, is typical of late Byzantine commentary manuscripts.
provenance: Its leaves are now divided between four libraries.
summary: A dispersed 9th-century commentary manuscript that preserves John 1:1.

name: Uncial 0290
contents_summary: Eight leaves with John 18:4–20:2.
dating_evidence: Written in a late majuscule (from about 800, most new Greek books were in minuscule, and majuscule was kept mainly for liturgical Gospel books). The date rests on comparison with a handful of dated majuscules (for example Vat. gr. 1666, dated 800, and 028 S, dated 949) and on features such as routine accents and breathings, heavy thick–thin contrast and liturgical reading marks. No dedicated recent dating study was found for this manuscript; the date is the INTF catalogue’s.
provenance: Discovered at St Catherine’s Monastery in May 1975. One published description gives the material as paper, which would be unusual for this date; this needs confirming.
summary: One of the manuscripts found in 1975, when a sealed room was opened during restoration work at St Catherine’s (the ‘New Finds’).

name: Codex Athous Lavrensis

date.label: 9th–10th century
date.summary: Palaeographic proposals run from the 8th to the 10th century; INTF: 9th/10th. Included here because much of that range falls before 900.

contents_summary: Gospels from Mark 9:5 onward, Acts, Catholic Epistles and Paul. John is complete.
dating_evidence: Proposals run from the 8th to the 10th century. Its late majuscule has been read in different ways, and there is no colophon to settle the question.

scholarly_positions.claim: 9th/10th century.

provenance: Has remained at the Great Lavra on Mount Athos.
summary: Known for giving both the short and the long ending of Mark. Its text mixes older Alexandrian readings with Byzantine ones.

name: Codex Vercellensis

date.label: late 4th c.
date.summary: Late 4th century; tradition links it to Bishop Eusebius of Vercelli (died 371).

contents_summary: The four Gospels; John 1:1–21:25 present, some leaves badly damaged.
dating_evidence: The oldest Latin Gospel book. Its uncial script fits the late 4th century, and a long-standing tradition connects it with Eusebius of Vercelli. It was used for swearing oaths in the early Middle Ages, which damaged many pages.
provenance: Kept at Vercelli Cathedral since late antiquity.
summary: The oldest surviving Latin Gospel book.

name: Codex Sangallensis 1395

date.label: early 5th c.
date.summary: Early 5th century, within a generation of Jerome’s Gospel revision (383–384).

contents_summary: Fragmentary Gospels; coverage of John 1:1–18 still to map.
dating_evidence: The oldest surviving copy of Jerome’s Gospel revision, dated from its script to the early 5th century, probably copied in Italy. Its leaves were later cut up and reused, so it survives in pieces.
provenance: Fragments recovered from bindings at St Gall.
summary: The oldest Vulgate Gospels.

name: Codex Palatinus

holding.library: Castello del Buonconsiglio (most leaves); Trinity College Dublin; British Library

contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps; John 1:1–18:11 and 18:26 onward.
dating_evidence: A purple codex written in silver ink, dated from its uncial script. Its text is the ‘African’ form of the Old Latin, close to the Bible quoted by Cyprian of Carthage in the 3rd century, so it preserves a text much older than the manuscript itself.
provenance: Dispersed; most leaves at Trent.
summary: A purple Gospel book preserving the African Old Latin text.

name: Codex Corbeiensis II
contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps; John lacks 17:15–18:9 and 20:22–21:8; 1:1–18 present.
dating_evidence: Dated from its uncial script.
provenance: From the abbey of Corbie in northern France.
summary: A 5th-century Old Latin Gospel book from Corbie.

name: Codex Veronensis
contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps (John 7:44–8:12 lost); John 1:1–18 present, including the singular reading at 1:13.
dating_evidence: A purple codex in silver and gold ink, dated from its uncial script to the 5th century.
provenance: Kept at Verona since the early Middle Ages.
summary: The only Latin manuscript with ‘he who was born’ at John 1:13.

name: Codex Fuldensis

date.summary: Precisely dated: corrected by Bishop Victor of Capua, whose notes record finishing on 2 May 546.

text_type: Vulgate, with the Gospels as a single harmony
contents_summary: New Testament; the Gospels are woven into one continuous narrative in the form of Tatian’s Diatessaron, which opens with John 1:1–5.
dating_evidence: One of the few early biblical manuscripts dated by its own notes: Victor of Capua records reading and correcting it, finishing on 2 May 546.
provenance: Owned by St Boniface, who gave it to the monastery at Fulda in 745; it has stayed there since.
summary: A precisely dated 6th-century Latin New Testament with the Gospels as a harmony.

name: Codex Brixianus
contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps in Matthew and Mark; John complete.
dating_evidence: A purple codex dated from its uncial script. Its Latin text appears to have been adjusted towards a Gothic translation, and it is often studied alongside the Gothic Codex Argenteus.
provenance: Brescia.
summary: A purple Gospel book linked to the Gothic Bible tradition.

name: Codex Monacensis
contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps; coverage of John 1:1–18 still to map.
dating_evidence: Dated from its uncial script.
provenance: To be documented.
summary: An Old Latin Gospel book of the 6th/7th century.

name: Codex Usserianus Primus

date.label: early 7th c.
date.summary: 6th/7th century, most often placed in the early 7th.

contents_summary: The four Gospels, fragmentary; John lacks 1:1–15, so only 1:16–18 of the Prologue survives.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script; possibly the earliest surviving Irish book.
provenance: Named after Archbishop James Ussher, whose library came to Trinity College.
summary: Possibly the oldest surviving Irish manuscript.

name: Book of Durrow

date.label: 7th c.
date.summary: Second half of the 7th century is usual; both date and place (Iona, Northumbria, Durrow) are debated.

contents_summary: The four Gospels; John complete.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script and its style of decoration, which is compared with metalwork and other Insular art; there is no secure dated anchor.

scholarly_positions.claim: Standard introduction to the manuscript, its date and origin.

provenance: At the monastery of Durrow in Ireland in the Middle Ages; Trinity College Dublin since the 17th century.
summary: One of the earliest fully decorated Insular Gospel books.

name: Codex Amiatinus

date.label: before 716
date.summary: Made at Wearmouth–Jarrow; one of three Bibles commissioned by Abbot Ceolfrith (from 692), and taken by him towards Rome in 716.

contents_summary: The whole Latin Bible; John complete.
dating_evidence: Dated by history, not only script: Ceolfrith set out with it as a gift for Pope Gregory II and died on the way at Langres on 29 September 716, so it was finished by then. Giovanni Battista de Rossi identified it (1888) with the Bibles Bede describes, correcting an earlier belief that it was 6th-century Italian.
provenance: Reached the abbey of Monte Amiata in Tuscany; in Florence since the 18th century.
summary: The oldest complete Latin Bible, made in England.

name: St Cuthbert Gospel

date.label: c. 700–730
date.summary: About 700–730 (revised after the British Library acquisition in 2012; earlier placed in the late 7th century).

contents_summary: The Gospel of John only, complete, in its original binding.
dating_evidence: Its script matches the Wearmouth–Jarrow scriptorium that produced Codex Amiatinus, which anchors the date. Found in St Cuthbert’s coffin at Durham in 1104.

scholarly_positions.claim: Collected studies following the 2012 acquisition, including its date, script and binding.

provenance: Placed in St Cuthbert’s coffin; recovered 1104; at Durham until the Reformation; owned by the Jesuits (Stonyhurst College) 1769–2012; bought by the British Library in 2012.
summary: The oldest intact European book, a pocket copy of John.

to_check: Full citation for Backhouse’s early date
name: Lindisfarne Gospels

date.label: c. 715–720
date.summary: British Library: c. 715–720. Window 687–721 from Cuthbert’s death and Bishop Eadfrith’s death.

contents_summary: The four Gospels; John complete. A 10th-century Old English gloss runs between the lines.
dating_evidence: A 10th-century note by the priest Aldred names Eadfrith (bishop of Lindisfarne 698–721) as the scribe, which gives a window. Unfinished details suggest work stopped at Eadfrith’s death.

scholarly_positions.claim: Before 698, to mark the elevation of Cuthbert’s relics that year.

provenance: Lindisfarne, then Chester-le-Street and Durham; Cotton collection; British Library.
summary: The best-known Anglo-Saxon Gospel book.

name: Codex Rehdigeranus

date.label: 8th c.
date.summary: 7th/8th century; probably Aquileia, first half of the 8th century.

contents_summary: The four Gospels with gaps; John lacks 1:1–16, so only 1:17–18 of the Prologue survives.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script and associated with Aquileia in north-east Italy.
provenance: Named after Thomas Rehdiger, whose collection went to Breslau (Wrocław); now in Berlin.
summary: An 8th-century Old Latin Gospel book from northern Italy.

name: Book of Kells

date.label: c. 800
date.summary: About 800; whether made on Iona, at Kells or both is debated.

contents_summary: The four Gospels; John breaks off at 17:13. John 1:1–18 present.
dating_evidence: Dated from its script and decoration, and linked historically to the Columban monks who moved from Iona to Kells after Viking raids in the early 9th century.

scholarly_positions.claim: Standard modern study.

provenance: Kells, Ireland; Trinity College Dublin since the 17th century.
summary: The most famous Insular Gospel book.
